items.headline: Overheard on Reddit: Inconceivable?
items.body:
A fencer asked r/Fencing whether the Princess Bride cliff-top duel is "BS." The verdict: real names, made-up moves, great show.

The masters are real. Camillo Agrippa (1553), Ridolfo Capo Ferro (1610) and Girard Thibault (1630) left rapier manuals you can still read. Bonetti is most likely Rocco Bonetti, who ran a school in Elizabethan London; no book of his survives.

Commenters agreed the moves on screen aren't the masters' techniques. "Thibault does not, in fact, cancel Capo Ferro," one wrote. Another called it "perfectly fine theatrical fencing."

The script called for "the greatest sword fight in modern times." Bob Anderson, who fenced sabre for Great Britain at the 1952 Olympics and doubled for Darth Vader in "Empire" and "Jedi," choreographed it. Cary Elwes's 2014 memoir, "As You Wish," recalls weeks of training before filming and months more on location.

*Fact check:* The Cliffs of Insanity are Ireland's Cliffs of Moher, but the duel was shot on a set.

claim_check.fact: Sword master on The Princess Bride (1987); GB sabre, Helsinki 1952 (7th ind., =5th team); Vader lightsaber double in The Empire Strikes Back (1980) and Return of the Jedi (1983). Thread says 'England': he fenced for England at the 1950 Empire Games, GB at the Olympics.

As You Wish: Inconceivable Tales from the Making of The Princess Bride (Elwes with Joe Layden, Atria, 2014); trained with Anderson and Peter Diamond: weeks of intense prep, then months more on location

claim_check.fact: Establishing shots at Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare; the duel atop the cliffs was shot on a set (London)
Robin Hood's Stride, Carl Wark (near Sheffield), Cave Dale, Lathkill Dale, Haddon Hall

In Goldman's novel as quoted in the thread: the man in black opens with Agrippa (suits rocky ground), Inigo answers with Capo Ferro, the man in black shifts to Thibault, and Inigo falls back on Bonetti; the film reorders and condenses this. Not checked against the book.
